about: Birka (Björkö in the Mälar bay), one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/birka.md and the spine. A draft for the user to overwrite. Real persons: Herigar, Frideburg and Catla (Rimbert, Life of Anskar); everyone else is invented, because no craftsman or trader of Birka is named in any text. (?) = not checked on a page that was opened. R 19 = Rimbert's Life of Anskar, chapter 19, in C. H. Robinson's translation of 1921.

ports.summary: The one market town of the Svear: a few hundred people on a small island of birch and rock in a bay that is an arm of the sea, a generation old in 793, heathen, with no coin, no church and no wall worth the name. A merchant comes for furs in their winter coat, bar iron, antler combs and wax, and brings glass, wine, cloth and blades, which are weighed against silver on a folding scale and never counted. The king's hall is on the next island; here his prefect keeps the jetties, and nothing great is settled without the thing and the lots.
ports.seasons: The bay has no tide and freezes from early winter to about Easter: then the iron comes in on sledges from the forest country, the fur dealers do their business on the ice, and men and horses go about on bone skates and crampons. Ships come from the going of the ice to the autumn storms, and the town is fullest between late May and the middle of the harvest moon, when the thing meets if the king is there.

history.text: The town is laid out on the west shore of the birch island, about this year or as late as 790. Which king of the Svear founded it is not known.
history.source: en.wikipedia and sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (about 750); B. Magnus, Birka (Riksantikvarieämbetet 1999) and de.wikipedia 'Birka und Hovgården' (about 790); dossier 1

history.text: A young craft town under a king whose name no one wrote down: bronze-casters, comb-makers and bead-makers in small sheds by the shore, strangers lodging in summer, no priest and no coin.
history.source: Magnus 1999; sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (the radar survey of 2018: the first town packed with small workshops); dossier 1, 2

history.text: From about this year silver coins of the caliphs come down from the east and are cut and weighed like any silver (?).

Envoys of the Svear ask Emperor Louis for priests. The monk Anskar sails with merchants; pirates take the ships and nearly forty books, and he comes to Birka on foot and by boat across the waters between. King Björn receives him.
Herigar, prefect of the town and a counsellor of the king, is baptised and builds a church on his own family land. Christian captives in the town are glad of a priest.
After a year and a half Anskar goes home with a letter from King Björn to the emperor, written 'in characters fashioned after the Swedish custom'.
About this year Bishop Gautbert comes to the Svear and begins a church.
history.source: Rimbert 14 (Robinson 1921); the year is the translator's

history.text: About this year a crowd breaks into the bishop's house, 'not by command of the king', kills his kinsman Nithard, and binds Gautbert and drives him out. For nearly seven years there is no priest.

Between 845 and 851 the exiled king Anund comes with twenty-one Danish ships and eleven of his own while the king is away. The town offers a hundred pounds of silver; the Danes say each merchant in the place has more. The lots send the Danes off to a Slav town, and Anund gives the silver back.
history.source: Rimbert 19 (Robinson 1921); the year 847 is the game's, within Rimbert's span

history.text: About this year the hermit priest Ardgar comes. Herigar dies; the old widow Frideburg dies, having kept bought wine three years for her last hour; Ardgar goes home.
Anskar comes a second time, nearly twenty days in a ship. King Olof says the matter rests with the whole people; the lots and two things say yes, and the king grants a plot for a hall of prayer.
King Olof's Svear burn Seeburg in Courland and take ransom at Apulia, five days inland. After the lots there favoured Christ, some of the host keep a forty days' fast from meat.
In these years Catla, Frideburg's daughter, carries her mother's wealth to Dorestad for the poor, because 'there are here but few poor'.
history.source: Rimbert 20 (Robinson 1921); the year is the spine's (about 852-860 (?))

history.text: Before this year the abbot of Fulda is said to send two bells to the mission (?).
history.source: sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (not checked against the letter (?)); dossier 5

history.text: Anskar dies on the third day of February. The priests Erimbert, Ansfrid and Rimbert have served here in turn; after them the mission lapses.
Early in the 900s the town's rampart is enlarged with timber on top, and more than fifty graves of about 900 are built into it.
Archbishop Unni of Hamburg-Bremen dies here on the seventeenth day of September, when Ring is king. His body is buried here and his head is taken to Bremen.
history.source: Adam of Bremen I 62, as quoted in en.wikipedia 'Birka' and 'Unni (bishop)'; not read in full

history.text: About 940 to 950 a woman is buried seated in a timber chamber by the fighting men's hall, with sword, axe, twenty-five arrows, two horses, three weights, three dice and twenty-eight gaming pieces.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Birka grave Bj 581'; what she was is disputed

history.text: The latest coins found in the town are of about this year.
About 970 to 975 the people leave. There is no sign of sack or fire in the town; the fort burns about then. Why they left is not known.
About now a king's town, Sigtuna, is laid out further up the bay.
In the 1060s Bishop Adalvard of Sigtuna visits the place and finds 'hardly a vestige' of the town, and not Unni's grave.
history.source: Adam of Bremen, scholia, as quoted in en.wikipedia 'Birka'; not read in full

eras.text: A young heathen craft town. Small sheds packed inside a low inner bank, plank-laid lanes, stone-footed jetties, a slight fort on the rock. The far trade runs south and west, to Dorestad; the first white silver of the east turns up in traders' bags from about 800. No priest, no coin, no named king.

The years of the first mission. King Björn lets Anskar preach; Herigar the prefect is baptised and has a church on his own land; from about 832 there is a bishop, Gautbert. A handful of Christians, most of them captives and traders baptised at Dorestad, in a town that still asks the lots. Hedeby's new pennies arrive and are weighed like any silver.

The bishop is driven out and his kinsman killed. No priest for nearly seven years. Herigar keeps his faith alone and is jeered at for it at the thing. An exiled king comes with Danish ships and is bought off with a hundred pounds of silver. A bad time to be known as a Christian, and a good one to be known as a man with a ship.

Anskar's second visit: King Olof, the lots and two things allow a priest and a hall of prayer. Herigar and Frideburg are dead; Catla carries her mother's alms south. The host comes home from Courland with ransom. From 863 Dorestad is gone, and the western trade goes by the Danes' town on the Schlei.

No priest again, and nobody asks for one. The trade has turned east: furs, wax and people out by Aldeigjuborg, silver by the bagful back. Weights made to the eastern standard are in every booth. Larger houses begin to stand among the sheds.

The best years. The town's rampart is raised with timber on top and the fort is rebuilt; some fifty armed men, horse and foot, keep a hall on the slope below it, dressed in coats of eastern cut. Silk, carnelian and silver in the graves. In 936 a foreign archbishop dies here and is buried.

The eastern silver thins and worsens. The land has risen, the southern sound shoals, and plots stand empty. Household by household the people load their boats and go. No enemy burns the town; the fort burns about the time the last of them leave.

Grass over black soil, the grave mounds, and the bank. Ships pass on their way to Sigtuna and do not stop. On the next island the king's estate goes on; about 1070 its steward Tolir has a stone cut by the harbour there. A bishop looks for the archbishop's grave in the 1060s and does not find it.

sites.name: The stone-footed jetties
sites.see: A row of timber jetties on footings of piled boulders runs out into flat brown-green water with no tide mark. In front, clinker boats nose to the planks and bales of fur lie stacked under hides; behind, plank roofs climb the slope in rows and smoke stands over them; to the left the bare fort rock drops sheer into the bay. Mallets, gulls, a dog, and the smell of tar, fish and wet birch.
sites.source: Jetties on stone footings below the houses, goods probably stacked near them (Magnus 1999); a harbour facing north, the way in beset with hidden rocks (Adam of Bremen as quoted in en.wikipedia 'Birka'); a share of cargo to the king through the prefect is likely, not recorded (dossier 4): pay_toll here is that due, in kind.

sites.name: The lanes of the Black Earth
sites.see: Narrow lanes run up from the shore between wattle fences, planks laid over the mud, pigs and dogs at the refuse. In front a spare man sits in his doorway with a folding scale on his knee; behind him small plank and clay houses, eight paces by five, each with smoke seeping from the roof. There is no square: the selling is done in doorways and on the planks, and the soil underfoot is black.
sites.source: The Black Earth: about 7 hectares of dark soil, houses about 8 by 5 m in rows, wattle-fenced plots, planks over the mud, refuse in the lanes; no market square is known (Magnus 1999; dossier 2). The plots are the king's ground and holders pay him a due (Magnus).

sites.name: The strangers' booths
sites.see: On the flat by the north end of the shore stand the summer booths of men from elsewhere: turf walls with a sail or hides stretched over, a chest for a door-sill. A Gotlander mends a net, two Wends sit by grey pots of honey, a Frisian airs cloth on a pole. In the evening the cooking fires make one line of smoke and four tongues are spoken at once.
sites.source: Merchants and strangers lodging among the craftsmen's households (Magnus 1999); Danes, Northmen, Slavs and Prussians each year (Adam, as quoted in en.wikipedia 'Birka'); honey in grey Slav pots (Magnus). Booths of turf and sailcloth are the ordinary northern kind and are not dug here (?).

sites.name: The casters' and comb-makers' sheds
sites.see: Low sheds stand shoulder to shoulder just above the water, none bigger than a boat turned over. In one a caster breaks a clay mould off a hot brooch; in the next a man saws elk antler into plates and the dust lies white on his knees; a woman winds molten glass on an iron rod and drops beads into ash. Charcoal smoke, burnt horn, the tap of small hammers.
sites.source: Bronze-casters by the shore with moulds for oval and equal-armed brooches, comb-makers in elk antler, bead-makers (Magnus 1999); the first town packed with workshops, nothing over 20 square metres (sv.wikipedia 'Birka', the survey of 2018).

sites.name: The iron smith's yard
sites.see: At the edge of the houses, downwind, a roofed hearth and a stone anvil block. Bundles of bar iron from the forest country lean against the fence, still tied with the bast they were sledged in with. A smith draws out rivets one after another and drops them hissing in a trough; a boy works the bellows with his foot. Locks and keys hang on a peg to show what can be had.
sites.source: Smiths among the town's crafts; iron from the forest country to the north-west, sledged in over winter; many locks and keys (Magnus 1999; dossier 2, 4). The smith here is the role forge's; no smith of Birka is named.

sites.name: The slip in the hollow
sites.see: A stone-lined hollow on the shore with a timber slip running into the water, and a half-planked hull on it, pale new oak against black tar. Rivets lie in a wooden bowl, whetstones of grey slate by the adze, shavings ankle deep. Two wrights sight along a strake and say nothing; a third heats tar and the smell reaches the jetties.
sites.source: A stone-lined hollow on the old shore with a timber slip, used and unused boat rivets, slate whetstones and woodworking tools, announced in 2022 (en.wikipedia 'Birka'). Its years of use are not given (?): the game keeps it for the whole life of the town.

sites.name: The brewing-woman's house
sites.see: A house like the others but with benches along both walls and the hearth kept high. Skippers and craftsmen sit knee to knee with horn cups; a board with glass playing pieces lies between two of them and a third gives advice nobody asked for. By the fire a hoarse man speaks a verse and stops short of its end. Ale, mead that smells of lime flowers, smoke in the eyes.
sites.source: An ale-house is the game's (ale-house riddles at Birka: unlocks_793.json); glass playing pieces from Birka's graves (town_games_793.json); lime-flower pollen, so honey from south or east of the Baltic (Magnus 1999).

sites.name: The open plain
sites.see: A level field above the town, grazed short, with a low stage of planks at one side and beside it a shelter of cut branches for the chief men. When the thing meets the field is full of standing men and the talk is a roar; a white cloth is spread and the lot sticks are thrown on it where all can see. The rest of the year it is sheep and wind.
sites.source: 'An open plain' with a stage and a shelter of branches, near enough to Herigar's church for a lame man to be carried there (Rimbert 19); lots cast in the open before any great decision (Rimbert 19, 26, 27); 'the control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king' (Rimbert 26, Robinson 1921). Where the field lay is not known.

sites.name: The long house on the terrace
sites.see: Above the town to the east, on a levelled terrace, stands a long house twenty paces from gable to gable, older than most of the roofs below it. Inside, a long fire, benches, a seat with carved posts for the king's man, shields on the wall. From the door one looks down over every roof and jetty, and north across the water to the next island, where the king's own hall stands above its harbour.
sites.source: Longhouses of a better sort on terraces east of the town, one 20 m long and built about when the town began (Magnus 1999). That the prefect kept it is the game's guess (?). The king's hall at Hovgården on Adelsö is the diggers' reading, not Rimbert's (dossier 8); the king's gift-giving at table is Rimbert 26.

sites.name: Herigar's church
sites.see: A small timber house on the prefect's own ground, set east and west, with a plain wooden cross over the door and no bell before the 850s. Inside, an earth floor, a table with a linen cloth, one lamp. A dozen people stand close: two or three townsmen, a rich old woman on a stool, and thin men and women with cropped hair who weep when the priest speaks Latin. When there is no priest the door is still swept.
sites.source: Herigar 'built a church on his own ancestral property' (Rimbert 11); Gautbert's church from about 832 (14); a hall for prayer on a plot the king granted in 852 and a house bought for the priest (28). None has been found (Arbman looked in 1932-34: Magnus 1999); the game shows one building for all three. Hear_mass only when a priest is in the town: 829-831, about 832-845, 851-865.

sites.name: The grave field east of the town
sites.see: On the higher ground behind the town the mounds lie as thick as molehills under birch and pine, hundreds of them, low and green, the newest still raw earth. A woman sets a small flat loaf on one and speaks to it as to a neighbour. Further up a single great standing stone marks a grave older than the town. It is quiet here; the mallets below sound far off.
sites.source: Hemlanden, over 1,600 mounds; some 3,000 graves in six fields; most burnt and laid in a pot under a mound, with small flat loaves on the pyre (64 found); the dead asked for counsel at the mound (Magnus 1999). The standing stone on a grave of the early 700s stood on the fort rock in sight of the town (sv.wikipedia 'Birkaborgen'); the game sets it at the edge of this field's view.

sites.name: The fort rock
sites.see: The island's highest point: bare grey rock that falls thirty metres sheer into the bay on the west, closed on the land side by a half-ring bank of stone and earth with a timber breastwork. A watchman stands by a heap of dry wood, looking north to the king's island. From 900 on, a hall of fighting men stands on the slope below, and horsemen in belted coats of eastern cut come and go by the King's Gate.
sites.source: Borg: a bank about 350 m long with a timber breastwork and three gates, one called the King's Gate, the cliff closing the west; built in two stages, the first slight; watchmen could signal to Hovgården (sv.wikipedia 'Birkaborgen'; Magnus 1999). The garrison terrace, about 50 men, horse and foot, with mail, scale armour, locks, comb cases and nothing of women's, is tenth century (?) (dossier 2, 8): the game opens it from 900.

people.name: Holmfast
people.trait: Counts everything twice and weighs it a third time: furs east to west, silver west to east, and no word wasted on either.
people.want: A steady buyer on the Rhine for furs and wax, and Frankish glass and blades to take east.
people.fear: Short weight; and the ice coming early with his goods on the wrong side of it.
people.voice: Numbers first. Repeats your offer back to you slowly, then is silent until you raise it.
people.looks: About thirty-five in 793, spare, pale-eyed, a trimmed beard, a fur-trimmed cap and a belted coat of eastern cut, folding scales in a round bronze case and a bag of lead weights at his belt.
knows: what a timber of squirrel, a bundle of bar iron and a cake of wax fetch here this moon, and what they fetched at Aldeigjuborg when he left it
silver: how to nick it, bend it and weigh it, and whose weights in the town are light
who has a plot to let, and what the prefect takes for the king
which blades go east without hilts, and who asks no questions about them
the Englishman in his booth who tallies furs and reads other men's sticks

the scale against the stamp: each thinks the other's silver needs testing

his son's son, born four years before he died, who has the booth and the scale case after them both

the pilot who takes his ship out through the sound each spring, and is told nothing about her cargo

carries the messages of the Svea on the Curonian hill home for nothing, and is the only man who brings him an answer
the smith on the eastern river hilts his bare blades for a share paid in iron
the river pilot who has taken his ship up to the town ten summers running; he pays him on the bank, and they have never eaten together
Ihalempi, who speaks for the trappers, counts aloud as he does; he counts twice and lets her check

buys Toke's combs at the river mouth in Skane for the east, and counts them twice
buys cased combs for the east from the comb-maker at the Danes' fjord market, and counts the teeth
the dealer at the Danes' fjord market from whom he takes the young captives east; he pays on the day
paid a widow on the Rhine strand in advance for jars with a pattern of tin foil, and is still waiting for the jars
ordered forty green beakers on the Rhine through a Frisian and paid half; the other half and the beakers are both still there
