lines.greet: A Frisian. You have come twenty days for furs. Show me your silver first, and put it where we can both see the scale.
lines.greet_again: You again. Last time: three timbers of squirrel, one cask short of what you promised. I wrote nothing down. I did not need to.
rumour: Forty skins. I counted them at Aldeigjuborg and again this morning. Forty. Now weigh your silver where I can see the scale.
This is white silver from the east. No king's face, writing all round. I do not read it. I weigh it. It weighs well.
The iron came late over the ice this year. Whoever has bars at midsummer names his own price. I have bars.
I keep an Englishman who tallies. He cuts a stick faster than I count. He is not for sale by weight.
lines.saying: Count it twice, weigh it once more, and then shake hands. In that order.
lines.farewell: Bring glass next time, and blades if you dare. Come before the ice or do not come.

people.source: invented (the spine's cast.holmfast, the same facts). Men of Birka had been to Dorstadt (Rimbert 27); scales and weights lie in Birka's graves; partners in one ship were félagar (Magnus 1999). His son keeps the booth after him: the role forge makes the heir. Name: Holm- + -fast, both common on the rune stones of Uppland.

people.name: Grimulf
people.trait: A hall poet grown too hoarse for halls, who sells riddles and verses for weighed silver in the brewing-woman's house and remembers every face that ever paid him.
people.want: Silver for his old age, and one listener who can answer him back.
people.fear: That the verses will end with him: nobody in a market town has the time to learn them whole.
people.voice: Hoarse and slow. Stops a verse one line short and holds out his hand.
people.looks: Past sixty, tall and stooped, a long grey moustache and a shaved chin, an old blue cloak pinned with a ring of iron, a bundle of rune-cut sticks tied with bast under his arm.
knows: the second of the three wave riddles, which he sells; and who has her sisters
the lays of the old kings of the Svear, as he tells them, which is not as they tell them at Uppsalir
which skipper drank with which, and what was said after the third horn
where the king is this season, and whether the thing will meet

ties.note: they sat on one bench long ago in the Danes' hall; he asks after Ravn before he asks your name
trades riddles with the skald at Hleidr by any skipper who can carry a stick without reading it
the Vestfold skipper gives away the first riddle; Grimulf thinks a thing given is a thing spoiled
Vifast, the king's poet up the river, on whose bench he learned the trade; Vifast has the hall, the ring and a full voice, and Grimulf says he has the better memory
was paid for a verse on an honest dealer and is still looking for the second half-line
his sister's daughter, who feeds him when the ships are few
went one summer to Gotland to learn from Likbjorn what the pictures on the stones mean, and came home with three different answers
the ferryman on the Danes' fjord has the third of the wave riddles, and takes a crossing rowed for it where Grimulf takes silver

lines.greet: A new face, and a southern one. Sit. I have a riddle that costs six pennies' weight and a silence that costs nothing.
lines.greet_again: I know you. You paid, you listened, and you did not answer. Have you an answer now, or only more silver?
rumour: How is Ravn? We shared a bench in the Danes' hall before your beard came. He knew the answers then and would not say them.
A Vestfold skipper gives the first of the sisters away for nothing. That is why nobody up there values her.
The king's poet at Uppsalir has a gold ring and a full voice. I have what he has forgotten.
lines.saying: A verse is like a ship's plank: one missing and the whole thing lets in water.
lines.farewell: Go on, then. When you have the answer, say it to me and not to the Dane. I asked first.

people.source: invented. riddles_793.json: 'a skald of Birka' sells r-gest-22, the second of the wave riddles (set aegirs_daughters), for 6 d; the spine's hook riddle_road (rd_setter_known). The riddles are Gestumblindi's, from the saga of King Heidrek (Vigfusson and Powell 1883). After 828 the role forge makes another skald. Name: Grim- + -ulf.

people.name: Ragnvi
people.trait: A bead-maker with her own scale and her own silver, who can tell where a glass rod was drawn by the colour it turns in the fire.
people.want: Glass rods from the Rhine and the blue and yellow kind from the Danes' side; and to sell direct to the eastern skippers without Holmfast in between.
people.fear: A bad eye. She has burned the left one twice and works with her head turned.
people.voice: Quick and sideways. Answers a question with a price.
people.looks: About thirty in 793, small, strong forearms scarred with old burns, hair tied in a cloth, a strap dress on two plain oval brooches with a string of her own beads between them, a little folding balance on a cord.
knows: glass: which rods melt clean, which beads the Finns and the men of the east will give a marten skin for
which casters in the sheds pour sound bronze and which stretch it with lead
that the wasp-striped beads come from the Danes' market in the west, and who carries them
what the women of the town owe one another, to the grain

ties.note: he buys her beads by the hundred and sells them east by the ten; she has counted what that makes
they share a fence and a pig, and weigh each other's silver on feast days
the goldsmith at Hleidr takes her beads for the women's strings and sends back drawn wire
the weaver at the kings' seat: cloth down the river for beads up it, by any boat that will carry a bundle unopened
has never met the man who makes the wasp beads, and has spent ten years trying to get his yellow
the last caster of the old island; when his fire went out she found him a bench in the sheds
the girl from the old island, who came over in 800 knowing moulds and nothing about glass
Hegvisl of Gotland winds beads as she does; she sends him her failed colours to guess at, and he guesses right too often
has never met the woman who makes the eye beads on the eastern river; one came back on a Gotlander's wrist, and she has broken three of her own trying

lines.greet: If you have glass, speak. If you have only silver, speak anyway, but I will listen with one ear.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the green rods. Half melted clean and half spat. I will show you which half, so you can show your seller.
rumour: Holmfast pays me for a hundred beads what he gets in the east for ten. He thinks I cannot count because I do it quietly.
The caster from the old island has a bench next to mine now. He pours other men's patterns and says nothing all day.
A Wend brought honey in grey pots and would take only beads for it. Blue ones. He weighed them against nothing; he just looked.
lines.saying: Glass tells the truth in the fire. So do most people, but glass is cheaper to test.
lines.farewell: Bring yellow. Nobody here can make yellow that holds. I will know if it is the Dane's.

people.source: invented: bead-makers, glass rods, Ribe's 'wasp beads' in the oldest layers, women who owned weights and silver (Magnus 1999; en.wikipedia 'Birka'). The ties to Hleidr and Helgö answer places/hleidr.json and places/helgo.json. Name: Ragn- + -vi.

people.name: Fastlög
people.trait: Weaves patterned ribbon on a slotted antler comb for the edges of rich men's coats, and takes in a stranger's mending with the same care.
people.want: Silk thread, a finger's length of it at a time, and to know who taught the woman in Skåne who weaves on the twin of her comb.
people.fear: Her eyes going before her daughter has the patterns by heart.
people.voice: Unhurried. Talks while she works and never looks up until she has finished the pick.
people.looks: In her late twenties in 793, broad and calm, fair hair knotted under a linen cloth, a blue strap dress with bronze oval brooches, a needle case and shears hanging from one of them, a narrow band of half-woven ribbon tied to her belt.
knows: cloth: what Frisian weave is honest and what has been stretched on the tenters
who in the town is getting a new coat, and so who has had a good year
the skald's verses, most of them, since he is her mother's brother and eats at her fire
where a foreign crew can get a roof and a wash without being robbed

ties.note: her mother's brother; she feeds him and corrects his verses
a shared fence, a shared pig, and thirty years of each other's business
a woman in Skåne weaves ribbon on the same kind of comb; they have never met and each has seen the other's work
mended the English boy's one shirt and was thanked in a tongue she did not know; he carries her messages since
wove the bands for the prefect's cloak, and after 830 the edge of a cloth for his new god's table
Rodiaud's farm on the Gotland shore lodges her kin and is lodged here in turn; each sends the other the cloth and cheese she thinks is better

lines.greet: Mind the warp. You are the southern skipper. Your cloak is good cloth badly hemmed. Sit; I will talk when this pick is through.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. That hem held, I see. What have you brought me, and do not say cloth.
rumour: A woman in Skåne works ribbon on a comb like mine. A skipper showed me her band. Who taught her? Nobody here taught me.
Holmfast's foreign boy holds a tally stick like something he is afraid to drop. He was taught that somewhere with a roof.
My uncle has not finished a verse in my hearing for ten winters. He says the endings cost extra. I am his niece.
lines.saying: A crooked edge shows on the first day. A crooked man takes a season.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you see silk thread anywhere between here and your river, think of me before you think of your king.

people.source: invented: weavers and seamstresses (needle cases in the graves), bands woven for coats of eastern cut (Magnus 1999; peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 2). The tie to Åhus answers places/ahus.json (ahus.thjodvi). Her daughters keep the loom after her. Name: Fast- + -lög.

people.name: Herigar
people.trait: The keeper of the town and a counsellor of the king: baptised, with a church on his own land, blunt as a judge, and not to be shouted down at the thing.
people.want: A priest at Birka again after 845, and the town kept whole whatever it thinks of his faith.
people.fear: The town paying for his faith: when the exiled king came with Danish ships, it cost a hundred pounds of silver.
people.voice: Blunt; a townsman who talks like a lawman. States a thing once and waits.
people.looks: About fifty in the 840s, heavy, a grey beard, a fur-trimmed cloak with a ring pin, a small silver cross worn openly, a staff of office and storehouse keys; lame in one leg for a time, and then not.
knows: where a ship may lie and what the king's due is on her cargo
the mind of the thing: who will shout, who will follow, and what the lots said last time
who in the town is a Christian, which is few enough to name on two hands
the ways in from the sea, and how many ships a watchman on the rock can count before they reach the piles

ties.note: the same person
the monk who baptised him, and whom he does not see again
the two pillars of Birka's Christians; she is the richer and the harder
Frideburg's daughter; he stood for her when the crowd came to the bishop's house
an old caster woman from the old island who works for his household and will not take his faith; he has stopped asking
the young merchant who put most into the ransom and asked for nothing but that it be remembered
the Danish king whose ships and exiles are the town's nearest danger
Fastlög wove the bands for his cloak, and after 830 the edge of the cloth for his church's table; she did not ask whose table
as a young man he stood beside the old lawman at the kings' mounds and learned from him to argue in the rain
a young Birka trader who stood in his church before he stood in any other, and brings him the news of the Curonian coast

lines.greet: You lie where I say you lie. The king's share comes off first. After that, trade with whom you like and cheat nobody.
lines.greet_again: The Dorstadt man. Your jetty is free. Is there a priest on your river who would come north? I ask every ship.
rumour: They said my god could not keep off rain. It rained on them. Their shelter fell on their heads. One small boy and I stayed dry.
A hundred pounds of silver, and the Danes said each merchant here had more. They were right. I did not tell them so.
Seven years without a priest. I am carried to my own church on bad days and I walk out of it. Explain that at your leisure.
lines.saying: The king asks, the people answer, the lots decide. A stranger does well to learn the order.
lines.farewell: Go with a fair wind. If you meet the monk Anskar, tell him the door is swept.

people.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 11, 19 (tr. Robinson 1921): 'the prefect of this town named Herigar, who was a counsellor of the king'; the wager in the rain, the lame leg, the ransom. His birth year is the game's guess (?); he died about 851. The ties to people of other ports are invented.

people.name: Frideburg
people.trait: Rich, old and unbending: with no priest left in the town she keeps bought wine by her for three years, to be dropped in her mouth at the last.
people.want: Everything she owns given to the poor; and since Birka has few poor, carried to Dorstadt, where there are many.
people.voice: Dry and certain; quotes her own promises back to people.
people.looks: Past seventy, upright in a chair, a fine dark gown with silver oval brooches and beads of glass and carnelian, a small cross among them, a sealed jar of wine on the shelf behind her.
knows: what every household on her lane is worth, and which of them would hide a Christian
Dorstadt by report: its churches, its priests, its many poor
the price of wine in a town where only two people want it
who broke into the bishop's house, by name, and what became of each

ties.note: the same person
her daughter, who is to carry the alms
the other pillar of Birka's Christians; she thinks he argues too much and prays too little
one of his flock; she has not seen him since she was sixty
a priest of the upper church on the Rhine, known to her only by what skippers say of him
her mother's father's sister kept the hearth of the king's hall at the mounds: a far line, and the game's link (?)

lines.greet: You are from Dorstadt. Good. Tell me how many churches there are. Count them. I have been told three different numbers.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian again. Is the wine on your river still sold by the cask? I need very little, and I need it to keep.
rumour: That jar has stood on that shelf three winters. It is not for drinking. It is for one drop, on one day, and I will say which.
There are here but few poor. On your river there are many. My silver should go where it is needed and not where it is envied.
I know who went into the bishop's house. One of them took a book home. Ask in the town what happened to his household.
lines.saying: I said I would, and I have. Now you say what you will do, and I will remember it for you.
lines.farewell: Go safely. My daughter may need a ship one day. I have marked yours.

people.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 20 (tr. Robinson 1921): the wine kept three years; 'there are here but few poor'. Her birth year is the game's guess (?); she died about 851-852, after Ardgar came. The book taken from the bishop's house is Rimbert 18 (from memory (?)).

people.name: Catla
people.trait: Dutiful and practical: she does exactly what her mother asked, and when she and her helpers are weary she buys four pennies' worth of wine and goes on.
people.want: To give it all away in the right places and come home.
people.fear: The road: the way to Dorstadt is beset by pirates, and a woman with a heavy bag is easy to read.
people.voice: Counts aloud. Asks devout women, not men, whom she can trust.
people.looks: About forty, sunburned, a plain travelling cloak over a good gown, her mother's beads, a heavy leather bag she carries herself and keeps on her lap.
knows: what her mother's goods fetched when they were sold, to the half ounce
which skippers her mother marked as safe, and why
the few Christian households of the town and who among them can be asked for a bed
after her journey: Dorstadt's holy places in the order she walked them

ties.note: the same person
her mother, whose word she is carrying out
the prefect stood between her door and the crowd in the bad year
one of his flock at Birka
a widow's house on the Rhine such as devout women would send her to (?)
a woman at the Danes' town where the ships for the west change (?)
Holmsten bought her mother's good loom at a fair weight when everything was sold, and told her which skippers to trust
a woman of Dorstadt who walked the holy places with her, and poured the four pennies' worth of wine when the others were weary
if the Gotland chain falls in her years: a widow of the island who also carries a dead parent's silver; they understood each other at once

lines.greet: My mother marked your ship. She said: that one counts his crew before he counts his cargo. Is that still so?
lines.greet_again: You came back. Then I will say it plainly: I have a bag to carry to Dorstadt and I cannot swim.
rumour: She kept the wine three years. At the end a priest came after all, the hermit, and she had both. She would say she planned it.
Everything is sold. Houses, brooches, the good loom. It weighs less than you would think and more than I like to carry.
We were tired and I spent four pennies on wine. When I looked, the bag was full again. All but the four. I have counted it since.
lines.saying: Do the thing you were asked, in the order you were asked, and let God do the counting.
lines.farewell: God keep your keel. If you pass Dorstadt before I do, tell the women at the upper church that I am coming.

people.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 20 (tr. Robinson 1921): 'There are there many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people'; the bag found full again but for the four pennies. Her dates are the spine's (?); her death is not recorded. The ties in Dorestad and Sliesthorp are invented.

people.name: Holmsten
people.trait: Holmfast's grandson: the same scale case, the same two counts and a third weighing, but he has turned the house's trade east and wears a hammer and, since a voyage to Dorstadt, a small cross under it.
people.want: The eastern road kept open and a western buyer who still comes now that Dorstadt is failing.
people.fear: Being the one in whose time the house's weights were found light. And Danish sails off the piles again.
people.voice: His grandfather's numbers, said faster. Tells you what your father paid before he tells you today's price.
people.looks: In his thirties in the 850s, spare and pale-eyed like the old man, a short fair beard, a fur-edged cap and a belted eastern coat, the old round bronze scale case worn smooth, a hammer ring and a small cross on one cord inside his shirt.
knows: what your house bought and sold at this door in his grandfather's day, as the tallies have it
the eastern road as it now runs: what white silver, wax and marten are worth at each end
who paid what into the hundred pounds, and who found a reason not to
which households are Christian and which merely went to Dorstadt once
the weights his house left in pledge at Truso, and with whom

ties.note: his father's father, who taught him to count on squirrel skins
the heir of the spine's Holmfast: his son's son
put more than his share into the ransom at the prefect's asking, and was not asked what gods he keeps
bought her mother's good loom when everything was sold, at a fair weight, and told her which skippers to trust
the amber-cutter's house at Truso holds weights of his in pledge since her grandfather's day
the old dealer Vigmund's house on the eastern river held his grandfather's furs till the ice went; the tie is to the house, and he keeps it
heard him at the thing in 852 and thought him a man who kept his word, which is all he asks of a god's servant
Hallstein of the big house on the Northmen's street holds his furs under his roof till the ice goes, as the old dealers held his grandfather's
lets the young trader work from a corner of the booth, and is paid in news of the Curonian coast
the grandson of the man who stood on the rock beside him when the Danes' ships lay off the piles; the two houses keep the tie after both of them

lines.greet: A Frisian mark. Wait. Yes: my grandfather's tally has it. Glass, a cask short. You are that house. Show me your silver.
lines.greet_again: You are back before the ice. Good. Your father never managed that. Put the scale where we can both see it.
rumour: A hundred pounds, and the Danes said each of us had more. I put in nine. I had more. So did they all.
Your Dorstadt is not what it was, I hear. I go east now. The silver there has no king on it and needs no excuse.
I was at your river once and let a priest put water on me. It did no harm. I wear both. One of them will be right.
The widow's daughter sold everything and weighed it herself. I bought the loom. She did not shave a grain. Nor did I.
lines.saying: My grandfather counted twice and weighed once more. I do the same, and then I ask who taught you to count.
lines.farewell: Come while there is still a western road to come by. And bring the cask you owe from my grandfather's day.

people.source: invented: the heir the spine gives cast.holmfast ('his son keeps the booth after him'; the son between them is the role forge's). 'Birka contained many rich merchants', and the Danes said each had more than the hundred pounds (Rimbert 19); men of Birka baptised at Dorstadt (Rimbert 27); hammer rings and crosses in the graves (Magnus 1999). The nine pounds are the game's. The tie to Truso answers places/truso.json. Name: Holm- + -sten.

people.name: Vigmund
people.trait: A horseman of the hall below the fort who has ridden the eastern rivers and come back with a coat, a bow and a taste for board games.
people.want: A worthy opponent at the board, and news of the east from someone who is not trying to sell him anything.
people.fear: A quiet harbour. He counts the ships each summer and the number goes the wrong way.
people.voice: Says less than he means, and that slowly. Never raises his voice; moves a playing piece instead.
people.looks: A lean man with a clipped fair beard, a belted coat of eastern cut with a row of small bronze buttons and a silk band at the cuff, a fur-edged cap, a comb in a case at his belt and a leather bag of gaming pieces and dice.
knows: the watch: how many ships passed the sound this moon, whose they were, and which carried more men than cargo
the game of the king's table, and a riddle about it that he gives to anyone who beats him
the eastern rivers as far as he rode them, and what silver is worth where it comes from
where the foreign archbishop was laid in 936, which few now can point to

ties.note: his grandfather stood on the rock with Holmsten when the Danes' ships lay off the piles; the two houses have kept the tie
is named for the old dealer of the eastern river, whose kin fostered his grandfather; wintered twice in a house of that kin and still sends a comb each year
a Gotland steersman who lodges under the rock when he comes for iron, and beats him at the board one year in three (if the island's chain falls in his years)
his hall buys its mead from Holmfast's line, five generations on, and the tally is never quite even

lines.greet: You were seen at the outer skerries at first light. One boat, low in the water, no shields. Welcome. Do you play?
lines.greet_again: The southern house. Your father sat there and lost a silver ring to me. Sit. I will give you the first move.
rumour: Thirty-one ships by midsummer last year. Twenty-six this. I do not say what that means. I only count.
The silver from the east is thinner than it was. Bend one and see. My father never had to bend one.
A bishop of the Saxons died here when I was young. They buried the body and took the head home. I know the place.
lines.saying: The king piece is safe only in the corner, and he cannot get there alone.
lines.farewell: Keep the split rock to your left going out. And think about your fourth move. It was where you lost.

people.source: invented: a man of the tenth-century garrison (about 50 men, horse and foot, with comb cases, locks and eastern gear: Magnus 1999; sv.wikipedia 'Birkaborgen'). riddles_793.json gives the tafl riddle to 'a man of Birka's garrison with a gaming bag'; grave Bj 581 held 28 pieces and three dice. The coat with small bronze buttons is Geijer 1938 (?), the one place a button is right (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 2). Name: Vig- + -mund.

stories.title: Counted twice, weighed once more
stories.summary: At Holmfast's door the merchant first sees silver with the Saracens' writing, whole and cut in halves and quarters, and learns that north of the Danes' wall a king's stamp is worth nothing and a true scale everything. Whoever learns both reckonings can carry the east's silver to the Rhine, with Holmfast or in spite of him.
stories.picture: A doorway in a plank-laid lane: a spare pale-eyed man in a fur-trimmed cap holding a small folding balance at eye level, a cut quarter of a white coin in one pan and a Frankish penny in the other, a southern merchant watching the beam.

beats.text: Holmfast, or the son or grandson at his door, pours a bag on a hide: white coins with writing all round and no king's face, some whole, some cut in halves and quarters. He counts them twice and weighs them once more. It is the first such silver you have handled, unless the old island showed you first (sets sv_first_dirham).

He nicks one of your pennies, bends it, and says it is good silver and two grains light of what your king says. He will take pennies by weight only. He names what he wants from the Rhine: glass, wine, cloth, and a thing he does not name aloud.

Ragnvi the bead-maker, or the woman at her bench after her, shows you which casters pour weights that agree with one another. A balance in a tinned case and eight weights can be had for silver, and after that nobody here can short you (sets sv_scale).
The moneyer on the Rhine puts the white coin in the pot with the scrap. Foreign silver is silver, he says, less his cut. He would still like to know who found his pennies light.

A Gotlander and a Wend are going east in company at the next fair wind and Holmfast has a place in the venture to offer: one purse, shares by what each puts in, the reckoning when the ships come back or do not.
On the eastern river the white silver is as common as pebbles and furs are what it is counted in. What Holmfast sells for ten here he bought for one there, and the bead-maker was right about him.

On Gotland the smith Hegvisl melts the same white coin into bars without reading it. He sells Holmfast beads by the hundred string, he says, and Holmfast weighs every string: the one Svea who weighs as often as a Gute.

At the lake of the Este the Dane Ketil lays his weights beside yours without being asked. Holmfast lodges with him on the way to the Vistula, he says, and checks them every time. They have not yet differed.

endings.how: You put silver into Holmfast's eastern venture and kept the reckoning honest on your side.
endings.text: The ships come back before the ice. Holmfast lays out your share on a hide, counts it twice, weighs it once more, and for the first time does not test your scale against his. His son is told your house's mark.
endings.reward: A standing partnership with Holmfast's line (the félag): furs and wax at the eastern price less a share, for as long as the booth is kept; Holmfast as a fast friend, inherited at half by the heir.

endings.how: You bought your own scale, learned the weights, and went east past him.
endings.text: Holmfast hears of it within the month, as he hears everything. Next time he greets you with a price a tenth worse and a nod a little deeper. A rival who can weigh is at least worth talking to.
endings.reward: The eastern prices at first hand and no share paid; Holmfast cool toward the house for some years; the bead-maker and her bench a friend for good.

endings.how: You would take and give nothing but counted pennies, as at home.
endings.text: Nobody quarrels with you. Nobody deals with you either, except at the price for a man who must be weighed for. You go home with a light hold and a clear idea of what a king's face is worth past the Eider.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but a season. The moneyer at Dorestad approves (sv_moneyer_trusts may still be earned there); the north stays dear until the house learns the scale.

stories.reward: The flags sv_first_dirham and sv_scale; a price word on furs, wax and white silver at both ends of the eastern road; a partner or a respected rival at Birka.

stories.title: The man who holds a stick like a pen
stories.summary: Holmfast keeps an Englishman who tallies his furs and reads the marks on other men's sticks: a boy carried off from the holy island in 793, sold north and east, a man of nearly fifty when Anskar comes. The merchant who has followed the trail finds him here, and must learn what he himself wants before deciding what to pay.
stories.picture: The inside of a trader's booth stacked with bundled furs: a thin man in northern dress, hair grown out, cutting notches in a tally stick held between finger and thumb like a quill, looking up startled at a word in his own tongue.

beats.text: In Holmfast's booth a servant in northern dress notches a tally and holds the stick like a pen. He answers to no English name until he hears his own. Then he puts the knife down very carefully (sets lf_boy_found).

Holmfast will not sell him by weight. He names instead what the man is worth to him each year in furs not miscounted, and multiplies it by the years left in him. Then he waits. The weaver next door says the boy has a place here and perhaps more than a place.
His elder brother has the price of half of him saved in a sock and asks one thing: does he still say the psalms? You have to say what you saw: Latin only in his sleep, the weaver told you.

beats.when: year < 831 and flag.lf_boy_found and not flag.lf_ransom_paid
beats.text: Come too late in a year and the booth is shut: Holmfast has gone east for the furs and taken his tallyman with him. The pilot at the old island counted the oar strokes out.

When the monk Anskar says the first Mass in the town, thin people with cropped hair stand at the back and weep. One of them is nearly fifty, in a trader's good coat, and gives the responses a half-beat before the rest.
At the lake of the Este a Frisian who keeps the fasts by his own count has seen the boy: he lodged there with his master, crossed himself at the sight of a cross, and then looked at Holmfast.

On the eastern river the dealer Vigmund once offered Holmfast a timber of sable for his English tally-boy, and was told the boy was not for sale by weight. He thought the price fair. His own tallyman is a Frisian taken as a child.

endings.how: You paid Holmfast's price in silver or in blades and carried the man home.
endings.text: He is sick the whole way and silent past the Danes' wall. On the sands below the holy island he takes off his shoes. Holmfast counts furs himself that winter and miscounts by two timbers.
endings.reward: The thread's flag lf_ransom_paid; the standing of a man who brings captives home, in every English port and with every monk; the brother's thanks and a place in a minster's prayers. Holmfast cool for a year, then even.

endings.how: You paid for his freedom and let him choose, and he chose to stay.
endings.text: He keeps the tally for Holmfast as a freed man on a share, takes a wife from the lane, and cuts one stick a year for you to carry west: marks only a monk could read. In 829 he is the first at the door of the new church.
endings.reward: A letter each year to carry to the brother (a small sure payment and a tie that outlasts both of them); Tidwine as a fast friend at Birka who reads any stick or leaf you bring him; Holmfast friendlier, since he kept his tallyman.

endings.how: You found him, weighed the price, and left him where he was.
endings.text: Nothing is said. He goes on notching. When Anskar comes he is still there, and tells the monk that a Frisian once knew his name and sailed. The monk writes nothing down.
endings.reward: No cost. The brother at home is told the truth or a kindness, as you choose; the crew remembers which.

stories.reward: The end of the trail from the holy island: a man brought home, a man freed, or a thing known; and Holmfast's measure of you either way.

stories.title: Dry in the rain
stories.summary: For thirty-five years a handful of Christians hold on in a town that asks the lots: a prefect who stays dry at the thing, a bishop driven out, a hundred pounds of silver on the table, an old woman's jar of wine, and at last an old man who stands up and says that Christ has helped men at sea. The merchant from Dorstadt is the one stranger both sides know.
stories.picture: An open field under a black sky: a crowd of men soaked and crouching under a shelter of branches that is shedding its leaves on them, and apart from them a heavy grey-bearded man with a staff and one small boy, both standing dry in a patch of pale light.

beats.text: A barefoot monk has come in on foot and by borrowed boat, robbed of everything on the way, nearly forty books among it. King Björn asks his people and lets him preach. Herigar the prefect listens from the door for a month and then asks to be baptised.

Herigar has built a church on his fathers' ground. The people in it are few: himself, the widow Frideburg, some traders who took the faith at Dorstadt, and captives who have not heard Latin since they were taken.

The bishop's house stands open and empty. A crowd broke in, killed his kinsman, bound him and put him out, and the king had not ordered it. A book from the house hangs tied to a fence at the edge of the town, and nobody will touch it.

They jeer at Herigar at the thing for a god who is nowhere. He says: it is about to rain; ask yours to keep it off you, and I will ask mine. It rains. Their shelter of branches comes down on them. He and one small boy are dry.

The exiled king lies off the piles with thirty-two ships and the king is away. A hundred pounds of silver is on the table and the Danes say every merchant here has more. Herigar asks what each man will put in, and looks at you with the rest.

Frideburg wants wine: a little, sound, in a vessel that will keep it. No priest may ever come again, and she means to have one drop of it in her mouth when she dies, in place of what a priest would bring.

Anskar has come again. A man says the gods have met and will take dead King Eric among them if the Svear want more gods. The king says it is for the people. The lots are thrown on the cloth, and an old man gets to his feet.

Frideburg is dead. Her daughter Catla has sold the houses, the brooches and the good loom, and has it all in one bag. Her mother said there are few poor here and many at Dorstadt. She asks what a Frisian boat charges for a woman who cannot swim.

A sunburned Svea woman is led round the holy places of your own town by devout women, giving silver from a bag. When they are weary she buys four pennies' worth of wine. Afterwards she counts the bag three times.

A foreign archbishop has died in the town at the turn of autumn. The body stays; the head must go to Bremen, and his clerks are asking along the jetties for a ship that will carry it and a skipper who will say nothing in harbour.

At the kings' mounds the story of the rain has arrived before you, and grown: there the prefect called the rain down himself. The old men remember that he learned to argue from their own lawman, on this mound, in worse weather.
Vigfast, a young Birka trader among the Curonians, tells the rain as a thing he saw. The man who lets him in by the day asks what such a god charges, and whether he keeps off anything besides rain.

endings.how: You stood with the Christians when it cost something: paid into the ransom, carried the wine, or spoke at the thing for what you had seen at Dorstadt.
endings.text: The lots fall well and the second thing agrees. The king grants a plot for a hall of prayer. The old man who spoke nods to you across the field: he, too, has been to your river.
endings.reward: The thread's standing with every priest from here to the Rhine; the right to found or mend the church (unlocks_793.json unlock_work_birka_church); the Christian households of the town as hosts for this house and its heirs.

endings.how: You spoke against the new faith, or made sure it was known you had no part in it.
endings.text: The town hears it and approves: a Frisian who knows his place among other men's gods. The priest is allowed in the end without your help. Herigar's kin remember exactly where you stood.
endings.reward: The good will of the town's heathen households and better prices from them for a generation; the Christians' doors closed; the church work is not offered.

endings.how: You traded, said nothing, and let the Svear settle their own gods.
endings.text: It is what most strangers do. Nobody thanks you and nobody blames you. Frideburg, if she is alive, says she had marked you for more.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost; the story can still be picked up at any later beat while it is live.

stories.reward: A place in the one stretch of Birka's life that was written down: the friendship of Herigar's and Frideburg's households, or of their opponents; and a late errand in 936 that Bremen pays for well.

stories.title: Blades without hilts
stories.summary: A Frankish blade is worth three times its price here, and more again on the eastern river. Holmfast buys them bare, without hilt or scabbard, so that they pack like bar iron and can be dressed to a buyer's taste, and sells them at Aldeigjuborg for furs and white silver. The emperor's law says none of this may happen.
stories.picture: The dim back of a booth: a long bundle unrolled from greased wool on a bench, six bright bare sword blades with naked tangs lying side by side, a pale-eyed trader testing one by bending it across his knee, a bundle of bar iron leaning in front to hide them from the door.

beats.text: Holmfast says the thing he would not name before. Blades. Bare, the tang naked, wrapped like iron bars. He will not ask where they came from and expects not to be asked where they go.
On the Rhine a smith's cousin has blades with a name let into the steel, and others with nearly the same name. Both leave by night. Only one kind bends and comes back straight.

The buyer at Holmfast's door bends each blade across his knee and lets it spring. Good ones he lays to the right. For those he pays at once, by weight of silver, about three times what they cost you (sets sw_buyer_known).

The iron smith fits a plain guard and pommel to one blade while you wait and hands it back. That is how they go east, he says: dressed here, in the fashion of whoever is buying, and no Frank would know his own work.
On the eastern river a blade from the Rhine buys a slave girl or two timbers of marten, and nobody has heard of the emperor's law or of the emperor.

The smith on the eastern river fits the hilts. He bends a blade against his knee, looks down it, and says nothing about where it was made: once his guard and pommel are on, it is nobody's business but the buyer's.
On the Curonian shore a Svea on the hill and a Curonian at the water both ask for the long iron, each out of the other's hearing. Holmfast carries the Svea's messages home, and brings him no blades.
A Gotland skipper going east will carry bare blades in his own hull for a share, sworn with a hand on the stone. He asks nobody at Birka, and Holmfast knows it.

endings.how: You brought blades north under the ballast and sold them at Holmfast's door.
endings.text: Three times the price, weighed and paid before the tar on your seams is dry. Holmfast asks for twice as many next year. On the Rhine a king's man is asking who buys so much greased wool.
endings.reward: Silver at three for one, and the thread's flags sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; Holmfast's trust and the eastern buyers' custom; the risk the thread carries at every Frankish toll from then on.

endings.how: You told Holmfast you carry no arms, and offered glass and wine instead.
endings.text: He repeats your answer back to you slowly and is silent. Then he says that a man who will not carry blades will at least not carry tales, and buys the glass.
endings.reward: No profit from blades; a clean name at the Frankish tolls; Holmfast's custom unharmed and a little slower.

endings.how: You carried what you learned back to the king's men on the Rhine.
endings.text: A smith's cousin is fined and a boat is searched. In the north the story arrives a season after you do. Holmfast weighs your silver a fourth time from then on, where everyone can see.
endings.reward: The count's good will and a mark in your favour at Dorestad's toll; wary faces at Birka and on the Schlei for some years (the news carries).

stories.reward: The best single margin in the north for a small boat, or a clean name; either way Holmfast knows what kind of man he deals with.

stories.title: The second sister
stories.summary: A hoarse skald in the brewing-woman's house sells the second of three riddles about Aegir's daughters for six pennies' weight of silver. He, a ferryman on the Schlei and a Vestfold skipper have all sat on a bench with the same Dane, and the answer to all three is under the merchant's own keel.
stories.picture: A smoky bench by a high fire: a tall stooped old man in a faded blue cloak holding out one open hand, a bundle of rune-cut sticks under his arm, horn cups and a board of glass playing pieces on the bench beside him.

beats.text: The skald speaks a riddle of maids who go many together to their father's joy and have brought grief to many, and stops one line short. The ending costs six pennies' weight. He will not be haggled with; he will be paid or not.
He asks after a Dane called Ravn before he asks your name. They shared a bench in the Danes' hall, long ago. Ravn knew the answers then and would not say them (sets rd_setter_known).
A Vestfold skipper gives the first sister away for nothing, as Grimulf complained he would.
The ferryman on the Schlei has the third. He takes no silver for it, only a crossing rowed by your own crew.
Say the answer to the skald in his own house and he finishes the verse at last, for the first time in his niece's hearing.

Vifast, on whose bench Grimulf learned the trade, has heard that his pupil sells the sea's daughters to merchants by the cup. He pretends not to know it, and asks what the second one fetches at Birka now.

Likbjorn the stone-cutter on Gotland remembers the hoarse skald from Birka, who came one summer to learn what the pictures on the stones mean and went home with three different answers. He would like to know which one Grimulf is selling.

endings.how: You gathered all three sisters and gave the answer to the skald at Birka first.
endings.text: He finishes the verse. The house goes quiet for it. Then he says he asked first and was answered first, and that he will say so to the Dane's face if he lives to see it.
endings.reward: The set aegirs_daughters answered (its reward for a ship, riddles_793.json); the skald as a fast friend, who sends a new riddle by any skipper bound your way; a seat by the fire in the brewing-woman's house.

endings.how: You gave the answer to the ferryman or the Vestfold skipper first.
endings.text: The set's reward is the same. Grimulf hears, and charges you double for the next one. His niece says he has been happier since he had someone to be angry with.
endings.reward: The set aegirs_daughters answered; the skald cool, and his riddles dearer.

endings.how: You paid for the riddle and never came back with an answer.
endings.text: He keeps your face and your silver. Each time you come in he looks up, sees there is no answer in you yet, and goes back to his cup.
endings.reward: The text of the second riddle in the chest (give_text of r-gest-22's text, riddles_793.json) and nothing more until it is answered.

stories.reward: One of the three riddles of the set aegirs_daughters, the flag rd_setter_known, and a man at Birka who will always ask whether you have the answer yet.

works.name: A fenced plot in the Black Earth
works.what: A strip of the king's ground running up from the shore, eight paces wide, with a wattle fence, a plank-and-clay house with a hearth on the floor, and a neighbour on each side who will know all your business by the second day.
works.needs: Enough Norse to bargain without an interpreter, the prefect at least easy with you, and a townsman to cut his mark as witness. Holmfast offers, and means to be the neighbour.
works.gives: A house of your own in the town: lodging and a small store without rent, goods sold from your own door, and a yearly due to the king through the prefect of sixty pennies' weight in silver or kind (unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_birka). Lost when the town empties in 975.
works.picture: A narrow fenced strip between two others on a slope above the water: a new small house of pale planks and wet clay, a man driving in the last wattle stake, a spare neighbour in a fur-trimmed cap leaning on the fence to watch.
works.source: The plots are the king's ground and holders pay him a due (Magnus 1999); houses about 8 by 5 m with wattle-fenced plots (the same). The price and the rate of the due are the game's (?); the sixty pennies' weight is as told on Helgö (places/helgo.json).

works.name: A jetty on your own stones
works.what: Boulders sledged out over the winter ice and tipped where the jetty is to stand, so that when the ice goes they are already in place; then oak piles and a plank deck on top, as long as your ship and a little more.
works.needs: A plot in the town first, and a winter: the stones go out over the ice or not at all.
works.gives: Your own berth below your own door: no waiting for a jetty in the full weeks of summer, loading without porters' hire, and room for a partner's ship beside yours.
works.picture: A frozen bay in low sun: a horse on spiked shoes dragging a sledge of boulders out from the shore toward a dark square hole cut in the ice, men with ice-picks, the snow-covered roofs of the town behind.
works.source: Timber jetties on footings of big stones below the houses; ice-picks and crampons for men and horses (Magnus 1999). Taking the stones out over the ice is the game's guess at how it was done (?).

works.name: A sledge and a stand on the ice
works.what: A horse sledge, a windbreak of hides on poles and a place on the ice off the jetties, where the fur dealers and the men of the forest country do the winter's business. Squirrel in its grey winter coat is sold here and nowhere else.
works.needs: To winter in the bay with the ship laid up, and one townsman who will say you are known.
works.gives: Furs and bar iron bought at the winter price, before any ship can reach the town; the hunters from the north learn your face, and the first choice of their skins is yours each year you come back.
works.picture: A wide white bay under a pink winter sky: sledges drawn up in a rough ring, bundles of grey squirrel skins on the ice, men in furs on bone skates, a small fire in an iron pan, the fort rock dark behind.
works.source: 'The only market place was the ice in winter'; fur dealers at winter markets on the ice; bone skates, ice-picks and crampons; iron sledged in over winter (Magnus 1999; dossier 2, 4). That the hunters were Sami is Magnus and en.wikipedia 'Birka'.

works.name: Your share of the pile line
works.what: A stretch of oak piles driven into the bay bottom off the jetties, close enough together that no ship can come straight in. After the exiled king's fleet lay off the town, every household with a ship is asked for timber or for silver.
works.needs: To have been in the town, or to have paid into the ransom, in the years the Danes came; or simply to be asked, as a man with a plot is.
works.gives: The town counts you one of its own: the prefect and his heirs are friendly without a gift, your ship is let in by the gap before strangers, and at the thing you may stand with the townsmen and be heard.
works.picture: Men on a raft of logs in still water driving a pile with a great wooden beetle, a line of pile heads already running away across the bay behind them, the jetties and roofs of the town on the right.
works.source: A line of piles stood in the water off the town to stop an attack; its date is not given (Magnus 1999). Setting it after Anund's fleet (Rimbert 19) is the game's guess (?).

works.name: The hall of prayer made good
works.what: On the plot the king granted in 852: a timber hall set east and west, a house for the priest in its own yard, a table for the altar, a lamp, and later a bell from the south if one can be carried so far.
works.needs: The lots and the two things to have said yes, a priest in the town, and enough Norse to deal with the wrights yourself.
works.gives: The Christians of Birka count you founder with the dead prefect: a bed and a table in their houses for this house and its heirs, a priest who will write a letter whenever one is in the town, and your name said at the altar (unlocks_793.json unlock_work_birka_church; works_793.json church_rebuilt, 40 d a year to keep).
works.picture: A small new timber hall with a wooden cross at the gable on a fenced plot among heathen roofs, a tonsured priest and a sunburned merchant holding the two ends of a measuring cord, townsfolk watching from over the fence without coming in.
works.source: Rimbert 28 (tr. Robinson 1921): the king granted a plot for a hall of prayer and Anskar bought a yard with a house for the priest. The two bells from Fulda before 856 are sv.wikipedia 'Birka' (?). No church has been found (Magnus 1999).

ships.note: The bay's own boat: clinker-built, four or five pairs of oars, light enough to drag over a neck of land or up onto the ice edge. Every household has one and somebody is always selling.
ships.picture: A slim tarred clinker boat lying alongside a stone-footed jetty, oars shipped, a woman with a folding scale naming a price to a man who is pressing his thumbnail into the top strake.
ships.source: The Mälar boat of 9 to 10 m (peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 6, after the Viks boat of about 1050, a later find standing in); ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The slip in the hollow builds a sailing and rowing ship of twelve to eighteen metres between one ice and the next: oak from the bay's shores, rivets from the smith by the fence, tar from the forest. This is the ship that goes east in company and comes back.
ships.picture: A half-planked hull on a timber slip in a stone-lined hollow, snow on the ground, two wrights fitting a strake with clamps, a bowl of rivets and a slate whetstone on a block in front.
ships.source: The shipyard with slip, rivets, whetstones and tools (en.wikipedia 'Birka', announced 2022); ships_793.json built_at includes birka; ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship.

ships.note: Wends and Prussians come each summer in broad shallow boats and now and then one of them goes home in a partner's hull and leaves his own for sale at the strangers' booths. Cheap, roomy, and no beauty to windward.
ships.picture: A broad low boat drawn half out on a flat shore by a row of turf booths, grey honey pots still stacked in her, a moustached man in a long belted tunic holding up fingers for a price.
ships.source: Slavs and Sembi (Prussians) at Birka each year (Adam of Bremen, as quoted in en.wikipedia 'Birka'); ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat. A sale of such a boat here is the game's guess (?).

ships.note: A pine dugout for nets and for crossing to the king's island in still weather. Sold for a sack of salt or a few bars of iron.
ships.picture: A long narrow dugout tied under a jetty among bigger boats, a bailer and a pike spear in her, a boy sitting in the stern eating bread.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat (cultures include svear); none has been found at Birka (?).

sayings.text: The control of public business of every kind should rest with the whole people and not with the king.
sayings.source: King Olof to Anskar, about 852: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 26 (tr. C. H. Robinson 1921). Said at Birka by anyone explaining to a Frank why the king cannot simply be paid.

sayings.text: Some of us who on various occasions have been to Dorstadt have of our own accord adopted this form of religion.
sayings.source: An old man at the thing of Birka, about 852: Rimbert 27 (tr. Robinson 1921). The one line in any text where the Svear speak of the player's own town.

sayings.text: There are here but few poor.
sayings.source: Frideburg of Birka, sending her alms to Dorestad: Rimbert 20 (tr. Robinson 1921).

sayings.text: Each individual merchant in the place had more.
sayings.source: What the Danes said of the hundred pounds of silver: Rimbert 19 (tr. Robinson 1921), the words as quoted in Design/content/dossiers/birka.md 7. Said in the town ever after, with some pride, of any price thought too low.

sayings.text: To question and answer must all be ready / Who wish to be known as wise; / Tell one thy thoughts, but beware of two, / All know what is known to three.
sayings.source: Hávamál 63, tr. Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), as given in Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj015. The rule of any félag of three.

sayings.text: He must early go forth who fain the blood / Or the goods of another would get; / The wolf that lies idle shall win little meat, / Or the sleeping man success.
sayings.source: Hávamál 58, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj014). Said at the jetties to a crew still asleep when the ice has gone.

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, / And so one dies one's self; / But a noble name will never die, / If good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Hávamál 77, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj019). Said at the mounds.

sayings.text: So may the gods be kind to me.
sayings.source: The heathen oath kept in the older Västgöta law, 'Sva se mær guþ hull' (about 1220, late; our gloss, as in peoples/svea_gotlandic.md 9). What a Svea says with his hand on the scale case.

sayings.text: The Frank asks whose face is on the silver. The Svea asks what it weighs. The silver does not care, and agrees with the Svea.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a Svea's understatement; the practice from the spine, silver_road)

sayings.text: A hammer and a cross can hang on one neck. It is the neck that gets tired.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; hammer rings and crosses both lie in Birka's graves (Magnus 1999)

sayings.text: Ask the gods, ask the dead, ask the thing. Then do what the ice allows.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; lots, counsel at the mound and the thing are Rimbert 19, 26-27 and Magnus 1999

sayings.text: They asked their gods to keep the rain off, and the gods sent leaves.
sayings.source: invented joke in the period's manner, on the wager in the rain (Rimbert 19): told by the town's few Christians, quietly

easter_eggs.text: A woman on the lane wears a silver ring set with violet glass, cut with marks like the Saracens' writing. Anyone who could read that writing would find that it says nothing at all. Nobody in the town can, so it is much admired.
easter_eggs.source: The ring from a Birka grave with imitation Arabic script (en.wikipedia 'Birka'; dossier 7). It does not prove any Muslim was here.

easter_eggs.text: A caster breaks a clay mould off a brooch and throws the pieces on the heap. A brooch from that same pattern will be put in a grave a hundred years later: the mould and its brooch were found a century apart.
The mead in the brewing-woman's house smells of lime flowers. No lime grows by the bay: the honey came in a grey pot from south or east of the sea, with a Wend.
easter_eggs.source: Lime-flower pollen in the town's dung layers (Magnus 1999); honey in Slav pots (the same)

easter_eggs.text: On the fort rock, in sight of every roof, stands a great stone over a grave older than the town: an old man and a small stallion. Nobody knows his name. The watchmen lean their spears on him.
easter_eggs.source: A grave of the early 700s under the fort with an older man and a small stallion, marked by a standing stone (sv.wikipedia 'Birkaborgen'; Magnus 1999)

easter_eggs.text: Under the door-sill of the long house on the terrace lies a middle-aged man with his weapons and half an elk antler by his head, and over him a younger man without his. People step across both every day and the older ones know it.
easter_eggs.source: Magnus 1999: the burial under the door of the 20 m house, the upper man beheaded and probably a slave

easter_eggs.text: One penny of King Charles with his name in a ring has found its way here and is kept as a curiosity, not as money. It will go into a grave with its owner.
easter_eggs.source: Grave 66 held a penny of Charlemagne; English and Frankish coins are otherwise rare (Magnus 1999; en.wikipedia 'Birka')

easter_eggs.text: The small flat loaves on the new mounds are baked for the dead and are no bigger than a palm. Sixty-four of them will last twelve hundred years.
easter_eggs.source: 64 small loaves from the cremation graves (Magnus 1999)

easter_eggs.text: From 900 on, a Christian woman of the town wears a small silver crucifix on which Christ is bound to the cross with cords, not nailed. Whoever made it had the story by hearsay.
easter_eggs.source: The crucifix of grave 660 and ten silver crosses from tenth-century women's graves (Magnus 1999; en.wikipedia 'Birka'). The site is closed by then; the game shows it on a woman in the lanes.

easter_eggs.text: In the 940s a woman is seated in a chamber grave by the fighting men's hall with a sword, an axe, twenty-five arrows, two horses, three weights, three dice and a full set of playing pieces. Ask Vigmund who she was and he moves a piece and says: someone who did not lose often.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia 'Birka grave Bj 581'. What she was is disputed, and the game does not say.

easter_eggs.text: A girl of about six is buried in these years with a brooch, a string of beads, a small knife and a needle case: everything a grown woman of the lane would carry, a third the size.

The wasp-striped beads in the oldest rubbish of the town were not made here. They came from the Danes' market on the western sea, in the first years, before the island had a bead-maker who could do stripes.
easter_eggs.source: Ribe's 'wasp beads' in Birka's oldest layers (Magnus 1999; en.wikipedia 'Birka')

easter_eggs.text: After 975 the island is grass. In the year 1871 a man who studies insects will come here looking for amber with flies in it, put a spade into the black soil, and find the town instead.
easter_eggs.source: Hjalmar Stolpe's digs of 1871-81 began as a search for amber (Magnus 1999; sv.wikipedia 'Birka')

unlocks.what: Silver of the caliphs, seen whole and cut, and weighed in your own hand
unlocks.how: Let Holmfast, or the heir at his door, weigh your pennies and show his bag, any year before 976.
unlocks.gives: The thread's flag sv_first_dirham if the house does not hold it yet (flag sv_first_dirham): dirhams are named in the hold and the market instead of 'strange silver', and the moneyer at Dorestad has something to say.

unlocks.what: A folding balance in a tinned case and eight weights that agree with the town's
unlocks.how: Buy them in the casters' sheds on the bead-maker's word, after the first white silver.
unlocks.gives: The thread's flag sv_scale (flag sv_scale): northern buyers stop shorting you; weigh_silver and test_silver cost nothing wherever silver goes by weight.

unlocks.what: Holmfast's mark cut beside yours on a split tally
unlocks.how: End 'Counted twice, weighed once more' as a partner, or bring him brass, glass or blades three years running without one short measure.
unlocks.gives: A commission each spring for goods from the Rhine at a price fixed the autumn before (commission); furs held for you till the ice goes; inherited by your heir and his at half strength, as feeling is.

unlocks.what: A plot in the Black Earth
unlocks.how: Pay for the work 'A fenced plot in the Black Earth' with Holmfast or another townsman as witness.
unlocks.gives: unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_birka: a house and store in the town, your own door to sell from, and a neighbour who buys from you every year.

unlocks.what: A Christian household that keeps your goods
unlocks.how: Carry wine north for Frideburg, or carry Catla and her bag to Dorestad, and be friendly with that household.
unlocks.gives: unlocks_793.json unlock_factor_birka: a factor's house at Birka from 830, where a Dorestad merchant leaves goods to be sold in his absence.

unlocks.how: Pay the skald six pennies' weight of silver in the brewing-woman's house.
unlocks.gives: The riddle r-gest-22 in the chest (give_riddle r-gest-22), one of the three of the set aegirs_daughters; and the flag rd_setter_known (flag rd_setter_known) once he has asked after Ravn.

unlocks.what: The riddle of the king's table
unlocks.how: Beat the man with the gaming bag at the board, or lose to him three times with good grace.
unlocks.gives: The tafl riddle of the set heidreks_board (riddles_793.json: given by a man of Birka's garrison), and a standing game whenever this house lies at Birka.

unlocks.what: The marks for the ways in from the sea
unlocks.how: Come in three times without touching, with a pilot or without, or be told them by the watch on the fort rock once he is friendly.
unlocks.gives: Counts toward unlocks_793.json unlock_pilot_malaren: no pilot is needed between the sea and Birka (learn).

unlocks.what: A known face at the ice market
unlocks.how: Winter in the bay and pay for the work 'A sledge and a stand on the ice'.
unlocks.gives: Furs and bar iron at the winter price each year you return, and the first word of how the hunting went, a season before any ship carries it south (news).

unlocks.how: Lie at Birka in the autumn of 936 and agree to carry the clerks and what they carry to the Schlei or the Weser, saying nothing in any harbour on the way.
unlocks.gives: A passage paid in silver by the church of Bremen (passenger, silver), the standing of a trusted carrier with every bishop's household on the North Sea, and a line in no chronicle.
